report:
**Conclusion: your “no” is too definite.** Monk’s pepper (chasteberry; *Vitex agnus-castus*) **may reduce PMS symptoms**, but the evidence is promising rather than conclusive.

A well-designed placebo-controlled trial followed 170 women for three cycles and found a standardized chasteberry extract improved overall PMS symptoms more than placebo. This supports a possible benefit, at least for that particular product and short treatment period. https://www.bmj.com/content/322/7279/134

However, the best synthesis of trials found that, although the pooled result favored chasteberry, the studies had substantial heterogeneity, high risk of bias, and possible publication bias. Thus, it could not make a definitive conclusion about effectiveness. This is important: “positive trials exist” does not mean all monk’s-pepper supplements reliably work, since preparations, doses, populations, and symptom measures differ. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28237870/

Current clinical guidance is similarly cautious. A summary of ACOG’s 2023 guideline says chasteberry was well tolerated and improved premenstrual symptoms in small studies, but ACOG did **not** recommend it because more study is needed. Established PMS/PMDD treatments have a firmer evidence base. https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/1200/practice-guidelines-premenstrual-disorders.pdf

Safety is not fully established for every situation. NCCIH advises that chasteberry can cause side effects and may be unsafe during pregnancy or breastfeeding; it may also interact with medicines that affect dopamine or hormones. Discuss use with a clinician—particularly if pregnant, trying to conceive, breastfeeding, or using hormonal/psychiatric treatment. https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/chasteberry
